utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Mitrovic. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry? I can hear the Albanian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mrs. Mitrovic? Thank you. I greeted you and reminded you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. And Mr. Cayley will now continue with his questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the witness please could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 54 ERN U003-2168.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher, could you put that on the ELMO for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, who is that, please?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my husband, Slobodan Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You can take it off the ELMO now. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we go back to this series of telephone calls that you were discussing yesterday. And we dealt with the first one that you received on the 17th of November of 1998, and you said in your evidence yesterday that you asked the caller where Boban was. And you stated that his response was: "On the other side." What did you understand the caller to mean by "on the other side"?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood him to mean that he was across the border, that he was not there in Kosovo. My first thought that he was probably in Skopje because this man spoke with a Macedonian dialect. So that was my first thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to the 18th of November of 1998, and this gentleman called you again. Can you recall now as you sit here as best you can the contents of the second telephone call?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that day, asked me whether I had been able to do anything about the passport and whether I would be able to come to Skopje to meet with him. I asked him -- I told him I was not able to get my passport. I asked him whether it would be possible for us to meet in the buffer zone and to speak. He told me that I was a very cold woman and said is it possible I didn't care about my husband. It was the exact opposite, because I didn't want my emotions to get in the way. He refused to come to the buffer zone. He insisted on my going to Skopje. However, he did not have any evidence and I was afraid. I told him that I could not believe that Boban was alive, since I had information that he had been killed. He then told me that he had seen him a few days ago and that he would be seeing him again. I then asked him, Well, is he still in Macedonia? He said, Ma'am, I did not tell you he was in Macedonia. I just said he was on the other side of the border. I asked him to make it possible for us to talk on the phone. He then said it did not depend on him but the people holding him, the guys down there. He said he would try to do something so that he be allowed to talk to me on the phone. And the outcome was that I would try again to get the passport. I told him to call me again at the same time, and I asked him if I was able to get my passport and if I was to walk into that restaurant he told me to go to, whom should I ask for. He just said that I should walk in and that I shouldn't ask for anyone, that he would recognise me. I asked him if we knew each other and he said that he knew me, that he had my photograph because Boban had given it to him. First he said that he had my photograph and I said, Well, I'm not a film star. My photographs are not everywhere. Then he said that Boban had given him my photograph. I was in a dilemma then, because I knew that Boban always carried my photograph in his wallet. The agreement was that we would speak to each other on the phone again the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, can I just ask you a couple of questions on what you've just said. You said that the man did not have any evidence. What did you mean by that? The caller didn't have any evidence.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, except for this word that he told me. He couldn't tell me anything else, anything about the whereabouts. If he had any letter or if he had been able to arrange for us to speak to each other on the phone, that would have been different. Then he said he didn't have anything to tell me, that he should hand over to me an envelope containing some demands. And when I said, What kind of demands? He said, When you see the envelope, when you read it, you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the gentleman caller said to you that he had your photograph. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was he able to describe your appearance from that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him, since he had my photograph, I said that I wanted him to tell me what I looked like. And then he said, Well, you're a woman. I said, Well, that's quite obvious; I'm not a man. Then I asked him if he knew any detail that would be striking in the photograph. And he couldn't tell me. He said, Well, just this: That you're a woman. And then I realised that in fact he did not have my photograph and that he probably knew me personally. Because if he had had my photograph, he would have noticed my glasses. I have worn glasses since my childhood; I never take them off. He may have said, Well, the only thing I noticed is that you're wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have any further conversations with this caller?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He called me again the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what did he say in that conversation, this next conversation, the next day?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he again insisted that I should go to Skopje. I said that I had been unable to get a passport and I also said that he had not given me any proof of the fact that Boban is still alive. Then I suggested that he should ask Boban, since he said that he was visiting him and that he would see him again, to ask him about some things that only Boban and I knew. And if he would be -- if he were able to provide me with an answer to that question, I would be prepared to go not only to Skopje but to the end of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the man prepared to do that? Was he prepared to ask Boban a question about matters which only which you and Boban knew about?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apparently not, because I never heard from him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Looking back on these series of telephone conversations, do you believe that Boban was in fact alive in November of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now you, I think, are involved with a number of missing persons organisations in Serbia, are you not?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you have contacts with other families, other Serbian families, whose loved ones are missing in Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your discussions with these families, have you been made aware that other families have received similar telephone calls to the series of calls that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many. In some cases money was sought for ransom, so that some poor people who had lost their family members have then lost money because they had paid thinking that they would be able to get their loved ones out of the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, based on your contacts with other Serb families, have any men who disappeared in 1998 turned up three, four years later alive in Kosovo and Serbia, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to very briefly direct you to a conversation that you had in May of 2004 with a man by the name of Adem Berisa. Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just very briefly describe that conversation.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a man from Suva Reka. We spoke on the phone. At one point he said that if late Boban were alive, he would be thinking and talking in a different manner. I was shocked. I asked him, Do you know that Boban is dead? And then he said -- he answered -- probably he was shocked himself by what he had just said. He said well he got confused because his Serbian was not good and that's why he said that. I don't think that that was the case, that he had made that mistake, because they all speak Serbian quite well because the term "late" in this sense is not something that you would use by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, you're living in Serbia now, is that right, today?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How is life for you in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how can the life of a person who had been expelled from her home look like, especially if you're a mother with small children, if you don't have a job, you're waiting for somebody to give you some charity? And you're unable to do anything. You can't even go back to look at your own home; you're not allowed to do that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And finally, I just want to ask you one last question. Six years have now passed since Boban disappeared. Today as you sit in the courtroom, do you believe him to be alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to be proven wrong and to be given a chance to apologise to everyone. But I do believe that he was killed, and that is why I'm here, because I want justice to prevail. And that those who committed that, that they be brought before justice and be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Mitrovic. I don't have anymore questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as indicated yesterday, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: We would thank her for attending court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Madam, I just have a few questions for you. I'll try not to keep you long. I hope that you'll be patient with me. Before trouble and then war came to your home, you and your husband and family were doing relatively well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Demonstrations, protests, and violence. Did you then, in 1998 and before it in 1997, appreciate why so many Kosovar Albanians were protesting?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth I never did understand that and I think they did not understand that. I had colleagues I worked with for 13 years. I was the only Serb among 13 Albanians in the rubber industry Balkan. When they went to demonstrate they asked me to look after their bags while they were protesting in the street. When I asked them why they wanted to protest they said they didn't know, that they were given an order. So they themselves did not know why they were protesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you become, aware as 1997 turned into 1998, that there were many Albanians losing their homes and their families and their lives, Kosovar Albanians, I mean?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just speak about the area where I lived in, not for the entire Kosovo. For the village of Recani, I know how they left their homes because those were they neighbours. They simply crossed the river which is located behind my house. And at that time they put up their tents and lived next to the river. That was their exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you telling us that they chose to live that way?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably done on somebody's orders. Because if you're a refugee, you cannot return to your home during the day and get some food and then disappear from sight in the afternoon. And that's precisely what happened in Recani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You know of no reason why your husband should have been taken. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because he was just a passenger. He was not armed, he did not wear a uniform, he was not on any front line because there weren't any front lines at the time. He was just an ordinary citizen. He was stopped on the road and kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He had, as far as you were aware, no enemies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all have people who like us or who dislike us. "Enemy," that's a very strong word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have friends who like you more and those who like you less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Had your husband as a successful businessman ever receive any threat to his well-being that you were aware of before he disappeared?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because there was nobody to threaten him. Our house was always open to members of all ethnic communities, especially to Albanians. We had them as our guests at our religious feasts. We saw in the new year with them. We never divided people in accordance with their ethnicity. We were not raised that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Madam, perhaps you might agree with me that as 1998 wore on and the war intensified, this was all over Kosovo a particularly lawless time. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean lawless time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Ordinary ideas of law and order, ordinary ideas of a civilised society were taking a back seat, weren't they, during this time of war. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as towns are concerned and the place where I lived, I think that there was law and order still.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Gangsters operating in the countryside, some of them acting under the umbrella of being part of a liberation struggle. Did you hear of such people and such groups in 1998, Mrs. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody had heard about that, not just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You received a number of what turned out to be very cruel messages and telephone calls, didn't you, over the months about your missing husband?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about a piece of information you were given, perhaps not by telephone. In your statement you refer to being told by two sources that there were kidnapped Serbs living in camps in Albania being made to do forced labour, loading and unloading ships. And this information was given to you, you tell the Tribunal in a statement, two years ago by two sources. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were these also telephone calls or people speaking directly to you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were these people you knew or people who just approached you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people that I personally asked and begged to find Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You told Mr. Cayley, the gentleman who was asking you some questions a few moments ago, about a missing persons organisation that you participate in. May I just finally ask you one or two questions about that organisation, please. Did you start in organisation or did you join it after it had started?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I organised one and I am cooperating with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you use, have you used the facilities of the Internet to communicate with each other?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are refugees from my territory, the territory of Kosovo. So we are all in Serbia. There's no need to use the Internet. We have meetings where we socialise, exchange information, communicate by telephone. There's no need to use the Internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May I ask you, Madam, the organisation that you began or came in at the start of, when did that start its meetings and work? Immediately after the disappearance of your husband or some time later?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organisation was founded right after we became refugees, in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: 1999. Thank you. Is your organisation - and you can only speak for yours - in contact with any Serbs who are living outside of the Balkans in other countries?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In the immediate days and weeks following your husband's disappearance, did you make contact with the office of State Security?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I went to all these institutions to report that he was missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- ranging from the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Yugoslav Red Cross, and the SUP, Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think one of the stories about your husband's disappearance that you received, is this right, is in early November of 1998 from the MUP in Suva Reka, and you deal with that in your statement to the Tribunal. Do you remember that story?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was going to town to buy something because I was living there with my mother-in-law. And I had to pass by the SUP. That's the road from my house. A patrol came along. A man came out of the car. The man was from Suva Reka, Novica. He said, You know, it's a good thing that I met you. I said, What's going on? He said, I'm just coming back from the checkpoint. It's the end of my shift. We have a man who was looking after the cattle and he said that he saw a truck full of refugees and he saw Miodrag Krstic among them. I was very upset, because I knew if one of them was there all of them had to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were able to pinpoint this account of a possible sighting of one of your husband's groups as being in November of 1998. Is that correct, Mrs. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You know, you grab at straws at such a time and you want to hear even impossible things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the awful position you were in was that you didn't know what was possible and what was impossible, did you, because you relied always on what others chose to tell you. Would that be a fair summary of the position you found yourself in, Mrs. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was kidnapped -- I have to go back, if the Chamber will allow me. When we found out when he was kidnapped, I told my mother-in-law, Don't moan so much. When they take him there and see who he is, they will return him home. These are all of his friends practically from childhood. And then as time went on, I could not understand that these friends and colleagues of his really meant to harm him. And because of the hope I had in that friendship, I wished to believe stories that he was alive. I repeat again: I wished that this was not true and I would want the opposite to be proved, that he was still alive. And in that case, I would offer a public apology to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You've been very patient with me. I have no more questions for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, Mr. Topolski asked you a question about a possible sighting of Miodrag Krstic in November of 1998. Do you recall that? You stated that a shepherd had seen Miodrag Krstic in a truck in November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was that sighting ever confirmed by anybody else, apart from this shepherd, the sighting of Miodrag Krstic? Could you speak up. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was, as far as you know, Miodrag Krstic ever seen again, apart from on this one alleged occasion?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say this. This is something that everybody knows. The only people who came out of that camp were the Bakracs, father and son. When I heard they were released - I saw that on the media and on television - we started to look for them immediately. They were found by Boban's uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because my question is very specific to you and it doesn't concern the Bakracs. As far as you know - as far as you know - Miodrag Krstic, apart from this one alleged occasion in November 1998, have there been any other sightings of him, Miodrag Krstic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much indeed, Mrs. Mitrovic. I don't have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitrovic, thank you very much. That concludes the evidence. We are very grateful that you have been able to come and assist us, even though it's very trying for you at this time. You are free now to return to your home in Serbia, if that's an accurate description. I know it's not the way you feel where your home is. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you could just excuse me for about five minutes and I'll be back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is an Investigator Birkeland. In a bundle of materials that we received last night from Mr. Whiting, who I think is taking this witness, is a document, part of which I wish to raise objection to as to its admissibility. I sought to obtain this morning the agreement of the Prosecution to omit it. There are two or perhaps three offending sentences -- or at least sentences that we find offensive. It has not been possible to reach any accommodation or agreement about it. Mr. Whiting, as of course he's entitled to do, indicates he wishes the whole document to go in. And consequently, in order for my objection to be heard, it was thought appropriate to raise the matter before Mr. Birkeland comes in to give evidence, which I apprehend may not be overextensive in length, I'm not really sure -- and for the Court to, as it were, rule upon it as to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems a practical course --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- save that we don't know what the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You're about to get it because it would be impossible for you to rule without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're asked to do many things here, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I haven't asked you to do the impossible. I can't pretend that I won't between now and the end of the trial. But today I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance on this matter. The document, I believe, was provided to the Court as well as Defence two days ago, not last night. It's part of the bundle of exhibits -- I stand corrected. It was at 2.00 yesterday. I apologise. But in any event, it has been provided to the Court. It's part of the bundle of documents for the next witness, L-67. And I believe you have the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder, Your Honours, could you please then go to this small bundle that's headed "Possible exhibits for use with L-67." The document I'm referring to is number 4. Its pagination is 0323-0952. And it's four or five pages in. It's an UNMIK international police document. "Supplement/continuation form."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At last, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope Your Honour's colleagues have it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What this appears to be is a note signed by our next witness, Birkeland, who as Your Honours will know is a police officer and an investigator, dated the 20th of September. And it looks to be, as it were, an internal document relating to a visit that he and a colleague made, and Your Honours see from the first two lines, in September 2000, to take a statement from a man called Xheladin Ademaj. He's a name we've come across already. He's the flour mill owner. I'm told by Mr. Cayley this morning -- and I'm not in the habit of referring to phone calls between counsel in submissions in court, but it is important that the Court to this extent should know the effect of that call -- it is anticipated that Ademaj will not be attending to give evidence. The note here goes on to deal with what he, Ademaj, said in a statement dated the 4th of July wherein he alleges that he was the victim of a kidnap. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We better go into closed session. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. This point -- this issue, this expression of fear by the witness and the connection of his to one of the accused, Isak Musliu, touches on the second, squarely on the second way that it comes into the trial, and to some extent on the third way. This witness -- the evidence will be that this witness is afraid to come to court to tell the story that he admitted to the investigator because he is afraid and he is primarily afraid of the accused Isak Musliu. Therefore, his fear, his reason for not coming to the court to tell the truth is directly tied in to the evidence, to the story that is going to be put before the Court. That -- it is the very reason why we have the investigator here to give the evidence, that -- the admission by this witness. And if you strip away the feeling of fear by Xheladin Ademaj, you strip away the whole sense of the evidence and why the witness is not here himself telling the account. He's not here himself because he is afraid. He admitted it to the investigator and that is what the investigator will put before the Court. So the fear and the reason for the fear is tied directly into the evidence that is going to be put before the Court and cannot be stripped away, cannot be sanitised. It is the reality. This is what the witness feelings. It affects his testimony. It affects him coming to court or not coming to court. For that reason alone I would submit that this evidence -- those sentences are relevant and are probative and should come in. I would submit that it also, perhaps to a less extent, but it also goes to the third point, and that -- about witnesses being told -- victims being told that they should not tell about what happened at Lapusnik. There has been evidence before the Court, as Mr. Topolski noted, that this Xheladin Ademaj was at Lapusnik. He was one of the victims at Lapusnik. Now, there -- I'm not aware of evidence that Xheladin Ademaj was specifically told, like some of the other witnesses, not to talk about his circumstances. However, I would submit that given the evidence that has been put before the Court by several witnesses that this was done repeatedly, I think it can be inferred from that evidence that this was a practice and the message was quite well-communicated to the victims at the camp. And I would submit that this witness's fear and unwillingness to come testify and come tell the truth about what happened corroborates that evidence. So it also to some extent goes to the third point. Now, Mr. Topolski complains that these sentences are both hearsay and that they are prejudicial. With respect to the hearsay point, yes, it is hearsay. And has been established from the very first day in this trial, hearsay is admissible. This evidence by its very nature has to be hearsay because Xheladin Ademaj is not going to come to court to testify that he is too afraid to tell the truth because he is too afraid to come to court to tell the truth. So the only way this evidence can come before the Court is by hearsay. Moreover, the issue is not whether it is prejudicial. Of course it is prejudicial; that's why the Prosecution is offering it. The question under Rule 89(F) is whether it is relevant, whether it is probative -- sorry, I didn't mean 89(F), I meant Rule 89. Whether it's relevant, whether it's probative, and whether the interests in providing a fair trial outweigh the probative value of the evidence. I would submit that the evidence is highly relevant, it's highly probative. The admission by Xheladin Ademaj to this investigator that (redacted) is telling the truth and that -- and to be candid, that admission is somewhat qualified and Your Honours will hear that -- and that he is too afraid to come to court to tell the truth about what happened to him is highly relevant and corroborates -- will corroborate witnesses who have already testified and witnesses who will testify in the future. There is nothing unfair about the evidence. There is nothing -- if the evidence is offered -- if it comes into evidence, there's nothing about it that creates an unfair trial for the accused. It is what it is. It is what the witness believes. It is what the witness feels. And it is reliable evidence, it's probative. It was obtained fairly. There is nothing that creates an unfair trial. Finally, with respect to the specific sentences, I would submit that they should all come in because they all tell the story. He says he is afraid and he's specifically afraid -- he explains his fear. And I don't think these sentences should be separated. It is one explanation. He explains he is afraid. He cannot tell the truth because he is afraid. He explains why he is afraid and that that is critical to his story. And the sentence about him being angry with the UN, that is just a further expression of his fear and his feelings about the accused Isak Musliu. The opinion in the last sentence is really just a restatement of what the witness Xheladin Ademaj told the investigator. So for these reasons I would submit that this evidence goes to the core of the admission that is made by Xheladin Ademaj to the investigator that we propose to put before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting's submissions place him in the position of an eloquent advocate on behalf of the missing Mr. Ademaj. One only has to stop and consider what it is Mr. Whiting is seeking to put in here to see the fallacy that lies at the heart of it. We are still in private session, are you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not at the moment. Do we need to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We should be. I said the name again. I thought we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: To have his statement placed before it in the various ways that might have been open to them in relation to a witness they knew was not going to come. One tentatively suggests that an attempt to have him before the Court under 92 bis would not have succeeded. There has been no application that I'm aware of of any kind, and therefore this is the mechanism by which this witness's statement, in part or in whole, is to be placed before this Tribunal. And what it is -- what is it that he says to Investigator Birkeland off the record -- in other words, I don't want to say this in public because I don't want to be asked about it in public -- behind my hand, I will whisper in your ear and tell you that I've lied. All of that can never be tested. What is it that the Prosecution now seek to put in? It really is a rehearsal by Mr. Whiting for the most part of a line of argument that began on the very first day of this trial and continues from time to time, although there has been something of a gap, to raise its rather ugly head again. And here it is under another heading: Fear/intimidation. As I said in my argument before Mr. Whiting responded, the very notion that this man's anger with the UN regarding the post-war job carried out by my client, that that can have any bearing whatsoever upon his guilt or innocence in this indictment is, we would submit - to be as polite about it as I possibly can - not an appropriate and sustainable argument. They could have taken steps; they haven't done so. This really is not just a lawyer's metaphor, a back-door attempt to get in some highly prejudicial material that, we repeat, has no probative value whatsoever. I'm being passed a note. May I just... Yes. I'm very grateful. We are not aware of any evidence or steps taken by the OTP to contact the witness who is not coming in recent times. We have no evidence beyond the 13th of September at 1200 hours of his current view, whether he continues to express and have the fears that he has in relation to Musliu in particular, or this case in general. We are now December 2004, four years after this meeting. Simply to highlight that as our final point, we would respectfully submit, underpins the valuelessness of this material and its prejudicial effect. Your Honours, they are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, the Chamber upholds your objection to the passages to which you've objected. The passages relate to the state of mind of a person who is not to be a witness, in 2000. If it could have any relevance, about which we don't express a view at the present, it would need to be the state of mind of that person at the current time. For reasons that have been put in argument, the statement in this objected passage is highly prejudicial. The Chamber considers that its probative value would be extremely limited, to put it at the highest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Given the time, it would seem more practical to break a little early and then to call the witness. So we will resume at 10 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may while the witness is being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As the Court is aware the Prosecution provided a bundle of documents it expects to use with this witness. The document which was the subject of some discussion before the break has been redacted and a redacted version has been provided to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, English is not your first language. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, but my second maybe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For that reason, I'm going to try to speak slowly and clearly, but if you don't understand any of my questions, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Also because we are both speaking in English and my questions and your answers need to be interpreted, we have to put a pause in between question and answer and then the next question. So I would just ask you first to speak as slowly and clearly as possible, and secondly to pause after my question before you begin your answer.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, are you presently a chief inspector in a police department?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm working as a chief inspector in a police department in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how long have you been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I graduated the police academy in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you start the police academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where are you presently assigned -- working?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I'm now at the moment in an EU mission in Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long have you been in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I started there the 19th January this here and I'll end the 20th of January next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What are your responsibilities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: My responsibility is to monitor, mentor, and to inspect the middle and upper management of the local police in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is my job down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What part of Bosnia are you in?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I'm in the north part, in the area called -- it's canton called Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Posavina canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, before this time in Bosnia have you had time -- have you had experience working in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. My first mission was in 1996 in the military. I was a sergeant, then a military police officer in Macedonia. And I was stationed in Skopje for one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I did all investigations concerning UN personnel and UN properties, investigations and securing of -- everything with the UN to do, everything. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what other investigative experience you have.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, before to Macedonia I was an investigator for two years before 1996. And then after 1996 I had one year. Between 1997 and 2000 when I went to Kosovo. So I had three years in investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Investigation experience?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes, doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said you went to Kosovo in 2000. Do you recall when in 2000 you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I went to Kosovo in June 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: One year, June 2001. One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to speak just a little more slowly, if you could.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you were in Kosovo, who did you work for?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I worked for the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: More specifically who did you work for?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: For a unit called CCIU and that means Central Criminal Investigation Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were your duties when you were working at CCIU?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: My unit was investigating war crimes happened before the NATO entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So war crimes that occurred before June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you investigate any other crimes or was it just war crimes?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: It was mainly war crimes. We also had major crimes because we have the whole Kosovo as our area. So if it was the major crimes that the departments couldn't handle, we had to take -- take it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the second half of your year in Kosovo, did you become a team leader?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you still working on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. I did the same work but I have only extra work as a team leader. I did investigation as I did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you were investigating war times, did you investigate alleged war crimes where Albanians were the suspects, where Serbs were the suspects, or did you do both?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I did both, but the majority was Albanians as suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the cases where Albanians were suspects, were the victims mostly Albanian, mostly Serb, or both?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: They were both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what kinds of crimes were you investigating specifically, what kinds of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: It was murders mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah. The files started with the missing person files and then became murder files.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there a separate missing persons unit?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so if I understand your testimony correctly, the missing persons unit would send to CCIU files of missing persons that they suspected were murdered?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimate of how many cases you would -- you worked on at one time during that year?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: The same time or during the whole year you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: At the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you can.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Ten cases maybe at the same time, maybe more. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now some questions about your involvement in the investigation of this case. First of all, were you involved in the investigation of this case?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall -- are you able to recall all of the investigative steps that you took during the investigation? In other words, do you have a clear memory of what you did step by step in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, but I wrote a log so -- but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show the witness a document which is contained in the bundle that was provided. It's ERN 0323-0765 to 0766.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the log that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. This is the log I wrote for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you kept this log.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I had it in my computer and everything I did with the case, I filled in this log.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you put it in as you did the -- as you took the steps in the case or did you do it all at the end?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No. I fill it in as I did it, the steps, not in the end but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As you did the investigation, you would update the log?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I updated all the time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the log contain all of the -- to your knowledge and your memory all of the investigative steps that you took in connection with this particular investigation?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. Except -- it's not mentioned that I received missing persons files. That is not mentioned. But when I started the investigation, everything is mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when you received the missing persons files?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: It was right before -- my first date in the log is the 11th of August. So I got the missing person files at the summer before, probably June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you received the missing person files and then subsequently or after that, you took these investigative steps?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, after you resumed that interview, did you then take steps to interview somebody by the name of Xheladin Ademaj?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. Xheladin Ademaj was mentioned in this witness statement from (redacted) and that's why I wanted to talk to him. So first I did ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah. If you could consult your log and --

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's the first thing you did to try to get in touch with -- try to interview Xheladin Ademaj?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: The first time I tried to interview him was the 9th of September, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I went to his village where he was living and to his house, and he was not at home. I talked to his daughter and arranged with her that Xheladin should come to my office in Pristina the day after, the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he come on the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: He didn't come the 10th of September either. So the 11th of September again I went back to his house. He was not home this time either. This was the 11th of September. And they are -- then I arranged with his daughter again to come back to my office in Pristina the 12th of September. And he didn't show up the 12th either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Younis needs the assistance of the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So he did not come to the office on the 12th of September?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Then the 13th, the day after that again, I was out taking a statement from another person. And then on the way back we drove to Xheladin's workplace. He owns a mill in the -- near of Ferizaj. We went to see if he was there. He was in the mill on the 13th and I took the statement from Xheladin that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'm going to show you a photograph. It's contained in Prosecution Exhibit 54 and it's U0038706.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, do you see that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah. This is Xheladin Ademaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The person that you interviewed on the 13th of September, 2000?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the interview as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I remember I took the statement from him, but I don't remember the details in the interview. But I remember I was there and took the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you write a report of the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. I write the report of the interview and also the next report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You wrote two reports?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I wrote two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the reports one at a time. But I'm going to need the usher to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the usher comes back, for the benefit of everybody else in the courtroom, I'm going to show you a document which has been provided to the parties and it's ERN 03230953 to 0956. The usher has returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I did this report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the -- is this one of the two reports that you prepared with respect to the interview of Xheladin Ademaj on the 13th of September?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a report I wrote about his story and what he want to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court how you prepared this report. That is, you've said you interviewed him on the 13th of September. How did you prepare the report? Did you do it at the time? Did you do it later?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: What we did when we -- my unit, we had the whole Kosovo as a work field and we have a lot of cases and what we did, we went around to the witness, took statements. Maybe we took statements from different cases the same days. And this day I took the statement from Xheladin. I also took a statement from another one. Out -- with the witness we took statement, I used the same form as I have in front of me, the witness statement form, and I wrote it with a pencil, handwriting. As it is -- this report here, only handwriting. And then we came to the office, wrote it in the computer and got it translated. And then we went back to get it signed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are you able to tell from this report or from you log when the witness signed this report?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: The witness signed this report the 21st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you -- in describing how this report was prepared you said you first wrote it in pencil by hand and then typed it. Is this typed report that is before you simply a typed version of what you wrote in -- by hand?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. We did it almost a hundred per cent proper out in the field, because we had a long distance to drive and we wanted to do it properly. Also sometimes we get it signed out in the field. They sign the handwritten forms also just to save time. And then we prepare it on the computer, print it out. And also the handwritten form is followed in those cases, not in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Birkeland, I believe you testified that you met the witness at his mill. Is that where the interview took place?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes, the interview and also the signing of the interview took place at the mill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall where the mill was located?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: It was outside Ferizaj, a town -- a small town called Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know specifically what village the mill is located in, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Petrovo. That is also where he had his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the house and the mill were in the same location in Petrovo?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. The mill was out on its own on a big field, not in the village, but out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the mill was in the field and was Mr. Ademaj's house connected to the mill or nearby?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, no. His house was in the village and the mill was out in a field connected to this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of a mill it was?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I think it was a mill producing wheat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The interview, do you recall or are you able to tell from your report who was present at the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I was together with one colleague of me. His name is -- yeah, it was the same officer who took the statement from (redacted) who joined me to this mill and took this statement and also a language assistant was together with me. And the witness, the four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there anybody else present from Mr. Ademaj's family?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, not at the mill as I can remember. Not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally how you conducted the interview.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: What I do when I take interview, I tell him what this is about, what he had to tell me about, and then he tell his story. And that's what he did here. He told his story to me and I wrote it down. And if there is something after, I ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean if there is something after?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: If there is some unclear thing in his story, I ask him some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking again at this report that is before you that you prepared, in this case did you ask -- after he told you the story, did you ask him questions?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him -- I asked him two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm not going to ask you to read the report, but could you just briefly summarise. And if you need to look at the report, that's fine. But could you just briefly summarise what Mr. Ademaj told you. And I would again ask you to take care to refer to any other person as "the other witness," if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, he stated in his witness statement that "On 4 July 1998 at 1200 Hrs 3 or 4 unknown masked soldiers came to my house in Petrove." Because of the uniform he saw, these soldiers were from UCK but he didn't recognise any of them because they were masked. And the soldier asked the witness if he gave wheat to the Serbs. And then the witness told that he gave wheat to everybody who was asking for it. Then the soldiers covered his eyes, put him in a car, and drove him away from his house. And then they drove him to a private house and put him in a small room. And he didn't know this -- the location of this house. And in this room he was sitting alone and I didn't -- he didn't see any other persons in this house. And it also says that once -- once they took him out from this room and faced to face to a UCK soldier, without mask. This UCK soldier asked him about his mill and if he gave wheat to the Serbs. And this soldier also asked him about weapons, if he had any weapons in his house. And he also said that he didn't know this soldier's name. Then he said nothing more happened in this house. And then after three, four days he was taken out from this room and UCK soldiers took him to a forest and told me that he had to go into the mountains. And then he travelled through Serbia and to Germany, where he stayed for one year and three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting. I thought as you were doing something else it may be a convenient time just to rise. My learned friend Mr. Whiting, of course, has asked that the witness summarise what was said. I think it would be useful to know whether or not he is simply reading a statement as part of his past recollection being recorded, or whether or not he's used that revive his present recollection; or if he's simply reading a document that he saw at a previous occasion. But I think -- it may be obvious, but may be useful for the record just to know exactly what the witness is doing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we pause I have just signed a redaction order for the name of the other witness, as given at line [sic] 15:16.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You might just clarify, if you would be so good, Mr. Whiting, the situation in respect of the memory of Mr. Birkeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can try to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, does this report refresh your recollection of what occurred at the interview with Mr. Ademaj? Does it allow you to remember what occurred then?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: When I read this statement I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to rise and interrupt. I'm afraid it's going to involve me giving a bit of evidence. The witness appears to have two documents in front of him, side by side. As I understood it, he was simply being asked to use one that Mr. Whiting put in front of him as a witness -- as a memory-refreshing document. I've been wondering why he's been able to add details like, for example, the words "at 1200 hours" after "the 4th of July," and I wonder if the other document he would be kind enough to indicate to Your Honours what is. I have my suspicions as to what it is, but perhaps he should tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The other document is the log which was put in front of him earlier. And 1200 hours appears in the document that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour. I don't believe that -- the question posed by Mr. Khan has yet to be answered. I believe that the videotape of these proceedings will show that thus far this particular witness has done a fair amount of reading of documents as opposed to testifying, which is perfectly fine if that's the way that Mr. Whiting seeks to elicit this evidence. And we're almost finished reading this particular document. There are but a few lines left. Then I suppose he'll be done with this aspect of Mr. Birkeland's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you just clarify, please, Mr. Whiting, that the second document is as you suggested, and whether the witness is simply reading from this statement or whether he is actually working on some aspects of memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, can you tell us what documents you have in front of you, please. There appear to be two different documents. Can you tell us what they are.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I have the witness statement from Xheladin Ademaj and the log I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what's the number in the upper right-hand corner of the document you've described as "the log."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's a two-page document?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what's the other -- what's the ERN number of the other document that is in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how many pages is that document?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: This document is also two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are there any other documents in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: This is the same document in Albanian language. And the picture of Xheladin Ademaj. And the witness statement from -- another witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, which was referred to previously?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when I was asking you to tell us what Xheladin Ademaj said in the interview, were you able to remember -- were you speaking -- let me put it this way: Were you speaking from your memory after looking at the report or were you just reading what's in the report?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I was looking and reading some sentences and some from my mind. I cannot remember details; too long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've substantially told us what -- according to the report what the witness told you. Do you recall what questions you asked him?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I asked him about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we're careful, I'm not talking about -- at this moment about -- anything about the other witness. Aside from any questions about the other witness, do you remember any questions that you put to him?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah. I asked him about this house he was put in. The UCK drove him to a house. He said in his statement he didn't know what it was. I asked him once more if he know where it was and if it could be in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you remember what he said?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: He said it could be, but he was not 100 per cent sure. But it could be, he said. And then I also asked him about -- if he knew who this commander was in this camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The commander --

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Commander of this area he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what area are you -- were you talking about? About what area?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: The Lipjan area. They have -- the UCK have fighting areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall what he told you in response to that question, who was the commander in the Lipjan area?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. He said the commander of the Lipjan area was Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, do you recall how long the interview lasted?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Between one and two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During this one- or two-hour period, did you talk only about the case or did you talk about other things?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: We talked about other things also. He showed me the mill, so -- he was very proud of his mill, so he showed me around this mill. We talked about a lot of things. He served us soft drinks and cake I think he came with. He was a very nice person to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if you recorded in your report the length of the interview or the beginning time and the end time?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the report and --

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- tell us if it indicates the beginning time of the interview and the ending time of the interview.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, it started at 12.00 and it ended at 13.30, so one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to your knowledge and your memory, was this report that you have before you that was later signed an accurate report of what he told you?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: This report here was a report that he want to sign. He also told me other things that he didn't want to have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But with respect to what he was willing to sign, is the report accurate?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've made reference to a second report.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, the second report was one report. I asked him some questions. After he wrote -- after he had gave me his story in the report he want to sign, I asked some questions because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be prudent now to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I would like the witness to be shown -- well, no -- in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, did you have occasion to interview Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes. I took one statement from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that interview took place?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: That interview was in the summer 2001, right before my end of mission. April maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would it help you to consult your log to get the exact date of the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Let's see. Yeah. The 24th of May, 2001, I took the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you prepare a report of the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now with the assistance of the usher I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 32, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many pages is that in front of you? Is that four pages?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Two pages in the English and two pages in Albanian -- three pages in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that the report of the interview you prepared?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: This is the report I did after the witness statement from Isak Musliu, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As you sit here today, do you have any memory of that interview?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: He was denying everything, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else about the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, not any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking at the second page of the document that is in front of you, is that your signature on the report?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: This is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And looking at the Albanian version of the interview, is the signature of the witness on that report?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps a few very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Birkeland, who gave you the missing persons log that you used to commence your investigations?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: It was not a log. It was separate cases that the relatives from the missing persons had reported to the missing persons unit. So it was reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You say that your investigations were focused on alleged crimes carried out by the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I was -- in my team we got most of the cases that was KLA as suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And for the second half of 2000, you of course were a team leader.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In the CCIU.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you hear about Serbs making allegations against various members of the KLA when you were in Kosovo in the year 2000? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: How many teams were there in the CCIU, do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: At the time I was there I think we were -- we were four or five teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Out of those four or five teams, how many teams were focused on investigating alleged atrocities carried out by the Serbs? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: All teams had cases with Serbs as suspects and Albanians as suspects. But my team had the majority of Albanian suspects cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: To give an approximation, if you remember, what percentage of your resources were focused on investigating allegations against the KLA as opposed to allegations against the Serb regime and Serb individuals? Do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I cannot remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And I suppose that in the course of your functioning as a team leader, you had regular get-togethers with other team leaders in the CCIU. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: We did not have regular meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You didn't get together, for example, once a month as a matter of normal management?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So people knew what was going on?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You've heard of the Qerez massacre in 1998, have you, in which various Albanian civilians were killed. Have you heard of that or not?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I cannot say that I can remember. I cannot say I can remember, no. But maybe I heard about it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell today?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The Likoshani massacre, have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Likoshani? I think I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You heard that various Albanian civilians were massacred. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That doesn't ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Prekaz, does that ring a bell or is that similarly lost in time?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I don't remember the names of the places the massacre was, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Let me try some others. Poklek massacre of Kosovar Albanians. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Obrinje, the Obrinje massacre, does that ring bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Ljubenik, the Ljubenik massacre, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Glogovac, that massacre, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The massacre in big Krusa and small Krusa, do those massacres ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You are of course a chief inspector today, aren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course spending one year in Kosovo you would no doubt have heard of the Jasari massacre in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You heard about the killing of 83 civilians?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That does ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I have long back in my head, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: How many women and children were murdered. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No, I don't. Not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the number 24 being raised?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember conducting any investigations at all into any of these massacres?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: I did not do any investigation of these massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: What was your remit in the CCIU? It was to investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: KAARE BIRKELAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
